If your Apple CarPlay connection drops while driving, the problem might not be with your iPhone, cable or car.

Unexpectedly, radio interference could be the culprit.

An Axios report once detailed a strange phenomenon in Boston—drivers would lose both CarPlay and Android Auto connections when passing through certain locations. Similar "signal dead zones" may exist in other cities, just not specifically reported.

The CarPlay head unit itself does not independently process GPS navigation—it simply connects to your iPhone via Bluetooth or Wi-Fi and projects the screen. When the wireless connection between the phone and the car's head unit experiences interference, navigation functions may fail and the connection may drop.

Mainframe's comment received the most likes

In Grapevine, Texas, when I drive along a stretch of road between an oil storage facility and a nursing home, all wireless CarPlay systems crash. I've tried many vehicles with factory wireless CarPlay, wireless CarPlay adapters, and aftermarket head units—they all crash on this stretch of road. Some systems recover on their own after disconnecting, while others simply cannot reconnect at all. Even the latest Mercedes-Benz electric vehicles have the same issue.

In the past decade, I've only experienced similar situations a handful of times.

Experts point out that nearby radio sources, especially interference in the 2.4GHz band, could be the cause. In Boston's case, speculation suggests it may involve point-to-point microwave links, broadcast antennas or unlicensed transmitters.

In summary, if you frequently lose CarPlay connection at the same location, you may be driving through an invisible zone of radio interference. The problem may not be solvable, but understanding the cause can at least save you a lot of time, avoiding unnecessary troubleshooting or repair appointments.
